newsitem.title: FRANCE: Iraq seen returning to world wheat market.
newsitem.headline: Iraq seen returning to world wheat market.

text.p: Further wheat purchases may be expected from Iraq, which went on a buying spree this week to celebrate its return to world grain markets, European grain traders said on Friday.
Iraq covered nearly half its import needs for the next six months on Thursday, buying 300,000 tonnes of wheat from France and 250,000 from Australia.
The wheat was bought with money raised from oil exports under a U.N. approved plan to provide relief from sanctions imposed after the invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
Traders said further purchases may already be in the pipeline from Argentina and Canada, and that Iraq is expected to shop for still more wheat in January to help cover import needs until end-April.
"I expect them to be back in January for March-April shipments," one exporter said.
This should lead to heated competition among major world exporters.
"Iraq may be willing to distribute (the purchases) among the main origins," one exporter said.
Australia, which was Iraq's biggest supplier before the Gulf war, has said it hopes to sell about 100,000 tonnes of wheat to Iraq each month.
One exporter put that target at 200,000 tonnes.
France which lent conditional support to Iraq's calls for a complete halt to U.N. sanctions, is also hoping to land further business.
But exporters said French wheat stood a chance only if the European Union granted the subsidies that would help it to compete against cheaper supplies from Australia.
They also said French wheat may not meet all the strict quality requirements demanded by Iraq.
Iraq is allowed to sell enough oil to raise $2 billion in renewable six-month stages under strict U.N. supervision while wider economic sanction continue to apply,
About half of the money raised will be deducted for U.N. costs, reparations and a special relief programme for Kurds in the north.
Total imports of wheat over the next six months could reach 1.2 million tonnes, Trade Minister Mohammed Medhi Saleh said earlier this month.
